---
order: 6
unit: drawing
moveId: read-for-the-job
reviews: [loop-block, name-a-value, loop-counter, value-update]
assumes: [repeat, variable, arithmetic, loop-index, variable-update]
title: A street of houses
summary: Read a whole program that uses loops and variables together, then change it and add to it.
language: python
app:
  command: node "$REPO_ROOT/tools/serve.mjs" "$REPO_ROOT/dist/_playground" 8123
  url: http://127.0.0.1:8123/index.html
  ready: Python code
  layout: full
pacing:
  keyDelayMs: 22
hook: "Real programs are longer than a few lines. Programmers spend more time reading code than writing it: they find the part that does a job, then change just that part."
---
There's nothing new in this program: it's loops, names, the counter and updates. It's just longer, so this time the skill is **reading** it: working out which part does which job, and how the parts lean on each other.

## Watch it built

```step
stage: info
app: true
query: { code: "", speed: 8 }
clip:
  - caption: "First, name the numbers the street depends on."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "from turtle import *\n\nspeed(0)\nhouses = 4\nwidth = 60\ngap = 20\n\n", append: true }
  - caption: "Move to the left of the screen without drawing."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "penup()\nbackward(220)\npendown()\n\n", append: true }
  - caption: "Everything indented under this line happens once per house."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "for house in range(houses):\n", append: true }
  - caption: "One house, part 1: the walls are a square."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "    # walls\n    for side in range(4):\n        forward(width)\n        left(90)\n", append: true }
  - caption: "Part 2: go up to the top corner, draw the roof, come back down."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "    # roof\n    left(90)\n    forward(width)\n    right(30)\n    forward(width)\n    right(120)\n    forward(width)\n    right(30)\n    forward(width)\n    left(90)\n", append: true }
  - caption: "Part 3: step along to where the next house starts."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "    # move along to the next house\n    penup()\n    forward(gap)\n    pendown()\n\n", append: true }
  - caption: "Last, work out how long the street is."
  - type: { into: "Python code", text: "print(houses * width + (houses - 1) * gap)\n", append: true }
  - click: Run
  - expect: { selector: "#status", contains: Finished }
  - caption: "Four houses, and the street is 300 long."
  - wait: 1500
```

Watch the program being built, one part at a time. Each caption names the job of the lines that follow it. You will need those jobs in a moment.

## Predict

```step
stage: predict
code: street.py#street
check:
  type: predict
  q: "Change houses to 5. What number will the last line print?"
  kind: number
  actual: "380. Five houses of 60 make 300, and the four gaps between them make 80 more: 5 × 60 + 4 × 20 = 380."
```

You saw it print 300 with 4 houses. Read the last line again: what changes when there is one more house?

## Run

```step
stage: run
code: street.py#street
try: { starter: "street.py#street", height: 420 }
check: { type: reflect, text: "I can point to the lines that draw one house, and the line that makes the houses repeat." }
```

Change `houses` to 5, run it and compare with your prediction. Watch the turtle: which part of the program is it running right now?

## Investigate

```step
stage: investigate
code: street.py#street
insight: "A longer program is made of parts that each do one job. Find the part, see what it depends on, and you can change it without breaking the rest."
tasks:
  - check:
      type: match
      q: "Match each part of the program with its job."
      pairs:
        - ["for side in range(4):", "draws the walls"]
        - ["left(90) then forward(width), right(30) ...", "draws the roof and comes back down to the ground"]
        - ["penup(), forward(gap), pendown()", "moves to where the next house starts, without drawing"]
        - ["for house in range(houses):", "repeats everything indented under it, once per house"]
      explain: "The outer loop repeats a whole house: walls, roof and the move along. The inner loop repeats only the walls."
  - check:
      type: number
      q: "Back to 4 houses. Change width to 70 and leave the rest. What will the last line print?"
      answer: 340
      explain: "4 × 70 + 3 × 20 = 340. Every part that uses width follows the change: the walls, the roof and the length."
  - check:
      type: bug
      code: street.py#bug
      text: "With houses = 4 this street looks right. Change houses to 6 and the roofs go wild. Click the wrong line."
      answer: 14
      fault: logic
      misconception: count-wrong-variable
      explain: "The walls loop repeats houses times instead of 4. It only looked right because houses happened to be 4. A square always has 4 sides, whatever houses is."
```

### Find the parts

Match each part with its job.

### Follow a change

What depends on `width`?

### Spot the bug

This version looks fine at first. Change a number and it isn't.

## Modify

```step
stage: modify
insight: "Change one part at a time and run after each change; the rest of the program should keep working."
try: { starter: "street.py#street", height: 420 }
tasks:
  - hint:
      - "The screen's right edge is about x = 250. The printed number is the street's length, starting from x = -220."
      - "Six houses need six widths and five gaps. Try a smaller width."
    check: { type: code, text: "Draw 6 houses that all fit on the screen.", rules: { contains: ["houses = 6"] } }
  - hint:
      - "Which line runs once per house? A change there happens to every house."
      - "Look back at size = size + 5 in A value that grows. Add a line at the end of the house loop."
    check: { type: code, text: "Make each house 10 wider than the one before.", rules: { contains: ["width = width + 10"] } }
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "After making the houses grow, I checked whether the printed length is still right, and said why." }
```

Change the street one step at a time. Run after each change.

### Six houses

Fit six houses on the screen.

### Growing houses

Make each house a little wider than the last.

### Is the length still right?

The last line works out the length from `width`. Is it still true?

## Make

```step
stage: make
try: { starter: "street.py#make", height: 420 }
tasks:
  - hint:
      - "Decide what one part looks like (one fence post, one tree), then what repeats."
      - "One post: turn up, go up, come back down, turn back, step along. Put those under a for line."
    check: { type: code, text: "Add something to the street that is drawn by its own loop.", rules: { loops: 3 } }
  - check: { type: reflect, text: "My new part uses a variable, so I can change how many or how big in one place." }
```

Add something new after the houses: a fence, a row of trees or a shop.

### Add a part

Give it its own loop, after the house loop.

### Make it adjustable

Give it its own variable, so how many or how big is set in one place.

## Lay a tiled floor

```step
stage: modify
try: { starter: "street.py#use", height: 420 }
```

Tilers plan floors like this: one tile, repeated. This program is a loop inside a loop, like the street. Which loop draws one tile, and which repeats the tile? Change the number of tiles, make them bigger, then add a second row.

```teacher
summary: Students watch a 30-line program being built part by part, then read it
  closely, change it and add to it. It uses only loops, variables and
  calculations from lessons 1 and 2; the new skill is reading a whole program.
time: 45
timing: Watch 5 min · Predict and Run 5 min · Investigate 15 min · Modify 10 min
  · Make 10 min
goals:
  - I can find the lines in a longer program that do one job.
  - I can say what changes when I change one variable, before I run it.
  - I can add a new part to a program without breaking the rest.
before: >
  Watch the build clip, then try the bug task with houses = 6. The bug (a loop
  that repeats houses times instead of 4) hides while houses is 4; that is the
  point of the lesson: parts of a program depend on each other in ways you only
  see when something changes.
running:
  - "Watch: play the clip once, whole class. Pause after each caption and ask
    what the next lines will do before they appear. The captions are the
    program's parts: name the numbers, move to the start, one house (walls,
    roof, step along), work out the length."
  - "Predict: students commit to the printed length for 5 houses before running.
    The common wrong answer is 400 (5 gaps instead of 4): ask them to count the
    gaps on the 4-house picture."
  - "Investigate: this is the heart of the lesson. The match and trace tasks are
    about parts and how they connect, not single lines. Ask: which lines would
    you change to make the roofs taller? (None alone: the roof is drawn with
    width, so it follows the walls.)"
  - "Modify: use the live slide to change one number together (houses to 6 shows
    the length growing), then students work on their own screens. They change
    one thing and run. The third task is a real question: after the houses grow,
    the printed length is wrong, because the formula assumes every house is the
    same width."
  - "Make: students work alone here; walk round, or use the live slide to build
    one part with the whole class. The new part needs its own loop and variable.
    Early finishers can make it depend on an existing variable (a fence as long
    as the street)."
stuck:
  - see: The houses are drawn on top of each other, or only one house appears.
    ask: Which lines move the turtle along, and are they indented under the house
      loop?
    fix: penup, forward(gap) and pendown must be inside the house loop, so the
      turtle steps along after every house.
  - see: The roofs point sideways or downwards after changing houses.
    ask: How many times does the walls loop repeat? Should that depend on how many
      houses there are?
    fix: A square always has 4 sides, so the walls loop is range(4), not
      range(houses).
  - see: A student's new part starts in the wrong place.
    ask: Where is the turtle, and which way is it facing, when the house loop ends?
    fix: It is at the ground after the last gap, facing right. Start the new part
      from there, or move with penup first.
stretch: Make the fence exactly as long as the street, using the same
  calculation as the last line.
support: Give the match task first on paper, cutting the program into its parts,
  before students touch the code.
leads: "This is the shape of every later unit: a few short lessons on new ideas,
  then a longer program that puts them together. Next unit adds decisions (if)
  and lists, and its programs grow the same way."
exit:
  q: The street has houses = 3, width = 50 and gap = 10. What does the last line
    print, and where does house 2 start if house 1 starts at x = -220?
  a: 170 (3 × 50 + 2 × 10). House 2 starts at -160 (-220 + 50 + 10).
explain: >
  A longer program is made of **parts**, each with one job. Here: name the
  numbers, move to the start, then a loop that repeats one house (walls, roof,
  step along), and a last line that works out the street's length.


  The house loop has a loop inside it: the inner loop draws the four walls, the
  outer loop repeats the whole house. Everything indented under `for house in
  range(houses):` happens once per house.


  The parts are joined by **variables**. `width` is used by the walls, the roof
  and the length, so changing it changes all three. That is why reading a
  program means asking, for each variable, "where else is this used?"
solutions:
  step-5#t1: street.py#sol-six
  step-5#t2: street.py#sol-grow
  step-6#t1: street.py#sol-fence
  step-7: street.py#sol-tiles
struggle: Reading a program longer than one screen. Ask students to say the job
  of each part aloud before they look at any single line.
class:
  inquiry:
    q: Programmers spend more time reading code than writing it. Is that a good use
      of their time, or a sign something is wrong?
    prompts:
      - Who reads your code besides you?
      - What makes a program easy to read? Is that the same as short?
      - Would you rather have a program that is short or one you can change
        easily?
    notes: "Expect both views. Reading is how you find where to make a change
      safely, so readable code saves time overall; but unclear code is a sign
      something is wrong. Come back to this at the jigsaw: which parts of the
      street program made it easy or hard to read?"
  activities:
    - at: start
      kind: info
      title: Today's program
      do: >
        Today's program is 30 lines long. It uses only loops and variables,
        which you already know.

        The skill today is reading: which part does which job?
      notes: "Play the Watch it built clip on the projector, pausing after each
        caption: what will the next lines do?"
    - at: investigate
      title: Jigsaw the program
      minutes: 8
      do: >
        Half the pairs read the walls and the roof. The other half read the move
        along and the last line.

        You have 3 minutes. Then find a pair from the other half and explain
        your part, line by line.
      notes: "This is Code.org's jigsaw from its Investigate lessons. Finish with the
        class naming the plan: repeat a unit, then step along. Ask where else
        they would use it (a fence, a row of tiles, a bar chart)."
    - at: investigate
      kind: discussion
      title: Two plans worth naming
      do: >
        **Repeat a unit, then step along:** draw one thing, move to where the
        next one starts, loop.

        **Work it out from the variables:** the last line calculates the length
        from houses, width and gap.

        Where else could you use each one?
    - at: modify
      title: "Optional: pairs at one computer"
      do: >
        Driver types, navigator checks the printed length after every change.
        Swap after each task.
    - at: end
      title: Gallery walk
      minutes: 4
      do: >
        Leave your street on screen. Walk round and find one street that does
        something yours doesn't.

        Back at your desk: in one sentence, what does your program do?
      notes: The one-sentence summary is the standard test of reading a whole program
        (explain in plain English). Collect a few aloud.
  questions:
    - at: investigate
      title: Follow the houses
      type: trace
      text: The first house starts at x = -220. Fill in where each house starts.
      table: |
        | house | starts at x |
        | 1 | -220 |
        | 2 | [-140] |
        | 3 | [-60] |
        | 4 | [20] |
      explain: Each house moves the turtle along width + gap = 60 + 20 = 80 before the
        next one starts.
    - at: investigate
      title: Why is this line here?
      type: question
      q: Inside the roof, forward(width) on the line after left(90) draws over a wall
        that is already there. Why is it needed?
      options:
        - It takes the turtle up to the corner where the roof starts
        - It makes the wall thicker
        - It is a mistake and can be deleted
        - It draws the roof
      answer: 0
      explain: After the walls the turtle is back at the bottom-left corner. The roof
        starts at the top-left, so the turtle has to get there first.
```
files.street.py:
# region: street
from turtle import *

speed(0)
houses = 4
width = 60
gap = 20

penup()
backward(220)
pendown()

for house in range(houses):
    # walls
    for side in range(4):
        forward(width)
        left(90)
    # roof
    left(90)
    forward(width)
    right(30)
    forward(width)
    right(120)
    forward(width)
    right(30)
    forward(width)
    left(90)
    # move along to the next house
    penup()
    forward(gap)
    pendown()

print(houses * width + (houses - 1) * gap)
# endregion

width = 40
gap = 20

penup()
backward(220)
pendown()

for house in range(houses):
    # walls
    for side in range(4):
        forward(width)
        left(90)
    # roof

from turtle import *

speed(0)
houses = 4
width = 60
gap = 20
posts = 8

penup()
backward(220)
pendown()

for house in range(houses):
    # walls
    for side in range(4):
        forward(width)
        left(90)

    forward(width)

    left(90)
    forward(30)
    backward(30)
    right(90)
    forward(10)
# endregion

# Two rows of six bigger tiles.

    for tile in range(6):
        for side in range(4):
            forward(50)
            right(90)
        penup()
        forward(50)
        pendown()
    penup()
    backward(300)
    right(90)
    forward(50)
    left(90)
